Fengxue Yanzhao owns the retained root: the founder's mind-seal is shaped like the mechanism of an iron ox — leave, and the seal pins you; stay, and the seal breaks you. And if one neither leaves nor stays — is it sealing, or not sealing? Can anyone say? The elder Luopi came out: I have the iron-ox mechanism — please, master, do not set the seal. Fengxue: used to hooking whales in the vast deep, and now he sighs at frog steps churning the mud and sand. Luopi paused — Fengxue shouted: elder, why not press on? Luopi went to reason it out — Fengxue struck him with the whisk: do you still remember the words? Try to raise them. Luopi went to open his mouth — Fengxue struck him with the whisk again.

Senses.Explanation: Leave and the seal pins you; stay and the seal breaks you: the iron-ox mind-seal that stamps both moves — raised from the prefecture office to the retreat's closing day. At the root, Fengxue Yanzhao in the Yingzhou prefecture office: the founder's mind-seal is shaped like the mechanism of an iron ox — leave, and the seal pins you; stay, and the seal breaks you. And if one neither leaves nor stays — is it sealing, or not sealing? Can anyone say? The elder Luopi came out: I have the iron-ox mechanism — please, master, do not set the seal. Fengxue: used to hooking whales in the vast deep, and now he sighs at frog steps churning the mud and sand. Luopi paused — Fengxue shouted: elder, why not press on? Luopi went to reason it out — the whisk: do you still remember the words? Try to raise them. He went to open his mouth — the whisk again. Chushi Fanqi, back from presenting tea at the provincial office, raised the case whole — leave and it pins you, stay and it breaks you; neither leaving nor staying — sealing, or not? — the elder Luopi: I have the iron ox, do not seal me — whales hooked in the vast deep, now frog steps churning mud — the pause, the shout, the whisk twice — and the herding lord: truly the Buddha's teaching and the king's law are one; cut not made at once, the confusion invites itself; Fengxue stepped down. Hongzhi Zhengjue's old-case section carries the same case to the same stepping-down, whale-hook verse and double whisk inside. Tianyin Yuanxiu raised it after his Luzu series: the founder's mind-seal like an iron ox — Luopi claimed the ox and asked off the seal — the whale-hook sigh at frog steps treading mud — the shout, the whisk, twice. Feiyin Tongrong, in his running comment on the Linji succession: NanYuan — bare flesh standing a thousand fathews sheer, unproved ones just look; then Fengxue: the seal of the founders and the sages like an iron ox — leave and it pins you, stay and it breaks you — and Feiyin's own verdict behind it: a great tiger wearing a paper hat — it startles you, and it makes you laugh. Daxiu Zhu, closing the retreat: a monk asked for the going-out sentence — watch your feet; then the master: leave and the seal pins you, stay and the seal breaks you; to neither leave nor stay — both are at fault. Assembly! how do you get free of this fault? a long silence — the four quarters up and down with nothing barred, east west south north with no crossing back.

Senses.Note: The saying advises care on a road while claiming that genuine going is no going. Feiyin cites it as he takes leave of his assembly. Miyin uses it during a move between teaching sites. Guantao tests it against his own return after many days away, and Wenmu calls the old caution too timid as he leaves a monastery. Their different journeys keep both halves of the saying active.

Senses.Explanation: An old travel saying pairs the act of departing with the claim that no departure occurs. Feiyin uses the tension at his own farewell and then leaves. Miyin makes it part of a discourse about moving his assembly without losing its source. Guantao applies it to his return from a long trip and asks what the staff has done. Senses.Explanation: Far from the sages in time — the corpus's standing diagnosis of a thin age, first sighed over Danxia and then turned against itself: no last phase of the way, no excuse at the eye's falling. The origin. Nanyang Huizhong, national teacher: Danxia comes to visit and has barely spread his mat when the teacher says — no need, no need. Danxia steps back three paces. Thus it is, thus it is. He steps forward three paces. It is not so, it is not so. Danxia circles the seat once and walks out. Says the teacher: far from the sages in time, men are mostly slack — thirty years on, to find even one man will be hard. Baofu's comment: Danxia hurried his journey and never felt his weariness. Foyan Qingyuan refuses the excuse the clause had become: nowadays, far from the sages in time, men are slack — the usual talk runs true phase, semblance phase, last phase. Says this mountain monk: the way has no true, semblance, or last phase — the way of the buddha is always in the world. Hit the moment and it is the true phase; miss the moment and it is semblance and last. You must resolve to settle this thing; the crux is getting out of birth-and-death — and birth-and-death was never there to get out of: seek it in the three times and it cannot be found. The past buddhas said it — the past mind cannot be got, the present mind cannot be got, the future mind cannot be got. Then who is the one, distinct upon distinct, listening to the way right now? And Gaofeng Yuanmiao, over the litany of the old hard years: ah — in the last phase, far from the sages in time, there is a whole breed of drifting types who simply do not believe there is a gate of awakening; they only bore on this side and reckon on that side. Grant the reckoning done and the boring finished — when the eyes fall to the ground, will any of it serve? If it would serve, why did the World-Honored One need six years in the snow mountains, Bodhidharma nine years at Shaolin, Changqing seven mats worn through sitting, Xianglin forty years to make one piece, Zhaozhou thirty years with no mixed intentions — why did they buy themselves all that suffering? Zhongfeng Mingben turns the clause into the reason the institutions exist: the earlier ones knew full well the direct pointing of no-letters-established — but because far from the sages in time, men's hearts sink day by day, their will to embody the way no longer close-grained, their consciousness chasing objects daily adrift — they had no choice but to rescue it. Before Baizhang built the monasteries, men went ragged and unwashed, lingering in empty mountains and great marshes, all-out for the way; by Baizhang's time there were already the old, the sick, the fearful — hence the monastery compound, to comfort the old and sick and support the way of the patriarchs. Had the elders not bent to the times and deftly set up the means, the two words direct-pointing would long since have died out unheard. Guting Shanjian, writing to the old pine monk: grieved for the grove's autumn season — far from the sages in time, everyone scrambling for snail-horn profit and fame, nursing hawk-stinking curds, not working on what is real, drumming up hollow heads; where they open their mouths, mostly book-drilling; when a thought rises, all dust-world opinions. Pile flowers and cluster brocade as they may, matching four-six into essays and pairing four-five into lines, holding mere mind-objects all the while — the true cause is lost entire; even should the root-light stir, they take the thief for their son. And Kongyin Daodu, writing to the scholar Huang: for the beginner the work is truly hard — no road ahead, the old dwelling lost behind, nothing to stand the foot on; none but the great-rooted fail to fall back. Add to it that far from the sages in time the demons are strong and the way weak: the few who incline to this gate take blessing-making and good works for the ultimate, flatly refusing to believe there is a truth of seeing the nature and attaining the way on the spot — one who hears mind-itself-is-buddha and does not turn his head is truly hard to find. Your wisdom outruns most — encourage yourself: the great matter of birth-and-death, the swiftness of impermanence — do not just chant it past as a line. Baiyu Jingsi, at the installation on Mount Shanqing: of late, far from the sages in time, the demons are strong and the way weak — Shanqing has come to this pass with no way out of it: he can only strip off the robe of jewels and don the tattered cloth, reach his hand into the market dust, drag through water and mud, hoping to find one man, or even half of one, to repay the buddha's kindness above and bring beings across below, set on keeping the true way circulating. And just at such a moment, how to celebrate? Two wheels, sun and moon, brighten the sage virtue; a hundred million mountains and rivers swell the royal design.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Livelihood and ordinary work do not conflict with reality
SearchAliases: livelihood and ordinary work do not conflict with reality
Senses.Note: The line says that livelihood and productive activity do not stand outside reality. Dahui uses it to reject destroying worldly forms to seek liberation. Yunmen cites it to an official who reads the Lotus and asks a question the official cannot answer. Yezhu asks why his audience gathers for a sermon but not for garden work. Chuiwan resists turning the saying into a fixed sectarian manner. Yuansou applies it to a gathered mountain community; Chushi asks what reality is and answers, above is sky and below is earth.

Senses.Explanation: To look toward and look up to someone or something is to regard it with reverent admiration. Weilin says a predecessor will be admired by later generations. Shanhui answers a monk’s praise of a revived monastery by allowing this respectful gaze. Shenfeng gives the phrase in a brief reply after a monk’s congratulatory words. Suru places the whole assembly in this posture toward what the master has just shown. Pufu says a visitor’s standing naturally draws respectful attention before turning to the present request for teaching. Yuanwu answers a question about how to approach someone with the phrase. Yulin gives it as a direct response to a question about an earlier teacher’s act.

Senses.Explanation: One sandal, westward home: the tomb opened and holding nothing but a shoe — read at memorials, portraits, installations, and pyres. Zhongfeng Mingben, in the encomium: that fellow cooked up wonders to repay a Chan debt — this land, that west, defeat upon defeat; he met the king of Liang and said 'no knowing', took Huike's three bows; chill and cold, one sandal returning west — the lacquered bucket still unlightened; banished to the lion-crag, mist-locked a thousand years — just watch whether the brow-hairs rot. Qianyan Yuanzhang, at the Founder's remembrance: nine years facing the wall cut off the whole world's tongues; one sandal returning west lost him his own poor life — 'I came to this land', and still the losing is not finished; 'to hand on the way and save the deluded', and still the cutting-off is not done — what, in the end? one flower opens five petals, the fruit sets of itself. Jie'an Jin, as the tablet enters the hall: nine years facing the wall — water rising from the high plain; one sandal returning west — sprouts rising from the ground; and how does the Founder arrive at Jinming? a glance left and right: carrying the bottle, dragging the staff. Guting Shanjian, seeing off a departing master: when Chan reaches the source, waking and delusion cease — the old foreigner's cleverness turned to clumsiness: returning west with one sandal, mud still on it. Wuqu Rukong, before the portrait: wide open, no sage; straight-out, no knowing — twice he lost his old capital in the hall of Liang, nine years of clean ash in the Shaolin room; at the last, a true man spares neither flesh, bone, marrow, nor skin — hands his whole body to others, shoulders the staff, one sandal returning west; old debts settled below Bear-Ear peak, a great wonder played on Onion-Ridge head — seen through by Song Yun — and then the whisk points at the picture: this one right here, who is it?; twice his red heart won no hearing; chill he trod the reeds away down the autumn river. Baishan Dekai, entering his monastery: at the Founder's shrine — the reed crossed the river, that was you; one sandal returning west, that was you; I thought how many tricks — bah, you were only here all along. Meixi Fudu, lighting the pyre: auspicious wood half-sky flying the north ridge, plum-blossom points on the southern sprays — in a flash heaven and earth flip their colors: one sandal returning west — just now.

Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yunwaize of Shending (神鼎雲外澤禪師語錄): The monastic questioner is unnamed: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shending Yunwai Ze (神鼎雲外澤禪師語錄): an unnamed monastic asks the purport of three catties of hemp; Shending answers separately.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records preserve “three catties of hemp” as Dongshan Shouchu’s answer to “what is Buddha?” and repeatedly reopen that answer for verse, comment, comparison, and interrogation. Dongshan Shouchu gives the original answer in his biography, and the Jingde Lamp Record quotes it. Wumen Huikai versifies it, Yuanwu Keqin places it among recorded Buddha-answers, and Zhongfeng Mingben pairs it with Yunmen’s dry shit-stick. Unnamed monastics later ask Ziyan Shangzuo and Shending Yunwai Ze for its purport. Their differing responses and Yuanwu’s rejection of facile explanations keep the phrase as a fixed case-answer rather than licensing an invented symbolic gloss for hemp or weight.
